extracted.intended_audience: scholars and critics of philosophy/sociology (reviewers responding to Spencer)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative points about how to criticise, interpret, and test philosophical and social-scientific claims, and how an author should be fairly represented in critical writing. Focuses on proper attribution, scope of tests, and precision of terminology in scholarly debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not refute statements not made
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism would be greatly diminished in bulk if there were excluded from it all that part devoted to disproving statements which have not been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure you are addressing the author's actual claims rather than a mis-stated or attributed position; avoid elaborately refuting positions the author never held. Example: Guthrie's work is described as largely a mis-statement of Spencer's views followed by a refutation of the mis-statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test aggregate laws on entire aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: The law is a law of the transformation of aggregates; and must be tested by the entire assemblages of phenomena which the aggregates present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating general laws (e.g., social evolution), do not base verdicts solely on detached groups of phenomena; examine the structures and actions of the entire society or the entire aggregate of societies to judge whether the law holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using isolated phenomena to disprove general claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Leslie's method is that of taking detached groups of social phenomena... and arguing that their later transformations do not harmonize with the alleged general law of Evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer failure of a general theory from counterexamples drawn from limited, isolated processes (language, fashion, trade); consider whether such counterexamples are representative of the totality to which the law applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge an author by their latest corrected expression
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usual in literary criticism to judge an author by the latest expression of his views... if he has made an error he should be allowed the benefit of any correction he makes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect authorial revisions; critics should not rely on earlier drafts or suppressed passages to indict the author if the author has replaced or corrected those passages in later editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not misattribute others' phrases as the author's
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting another's phrase as though it were mine is a literary misdemeanour... Mr. Mill's expression, quoted by Prof. Birks as though it were my expression, belongs to a theory of knowledge entirely at variance with that set forth in First Principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the provenance of quoted phrases; avoid tacitly or explicitly assigning another writer's wording or doctrine to the author under review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify and respect technical terminology and connotations
rubrics_metrics.description: The misleading connotations of the words 'appearance' and 'phenomenon' contribute to metaphysical confusion; had we used the term 'effect'... we should be in little danger of falling into the insanities of idealism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise with terms that carry popular vs. technical senses; identify and explain meaning used in the author's context rather than imposing a narrower or different common-sense meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid construing an author's stated conceptual stance as an ontological claim
rubrics_metrics.description: What is here said to be 'deducible mathematically from the relations of space?' Not a thing, or a force, but a law... Nothing is alleged respecting the existence of any central force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between asserting the form of a law (a mathematical or conceptual relation) and asserting the actual existence of the entities to which the law might apply; do not conflate laws with claims of existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume the author accepts doctrines they explicitly repudiate
rubrics_metrics.description: Prof. Birks tacitly implies that I accept the doctrine of Potential Energy... but I have repudiated this doctrine in the chapter on 'The Continuity of Motion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before critiquing an author's framework as dependent on a particular scientific or philosophical doctrine, check whether the author explicitly accepts or rejects that doctrine in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest and explicit about critical assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be but one opinion respecting the honesty of making the assumption [that Spencer accepted the doctrine of Potential Energy].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not proceed to elaborate criticisms that rest on unstated or unjustified assumptions about an author's views; if an assumption is necessary, state and defend it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid transforming meanings by selective quoting
rubrics_metrics.description: Prof. Birks quotes isolated words or short fragments in ways that lead readers to conclude I said things I did not say, thereby producing misinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote in context; avoid cherry-picking fragments that, when isolated, invert or distort the author's intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that methodological scope matters for validity of counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: The real question is, not whether we find advance to a more definite coherent heterogeneity in these taken separately, but whether we find this advance in the structures and actions of the entire society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim concerns systemic or aggregate transformation, evaluate examples at the correct systemic level—parts may behave differently from wholes; ensure counterexamples address the claim's intended scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer terms that reduce metaphysical ambiguity when addressing general readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Had phenomenon and appearance no such misleading associations... did we use the term 'effect,' which is equally applicable to all impressions... we should be in little danger of falling into the insanities of idealism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For communicating complex metaphysical points to general readers, choose vocabulary that minimizes misleading everyday connotations (e.g., 'effect' instead of 'appearance' where appropriate).
